opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people still think of these models primarily as text systems. You type something in, you get text back. That's been incredibly powerful, and it's surprised a lot of people, myself included in some ways. But it's a fairly narrow slice of how humans actually experience and understand the world.

When you start bringing in images, video, audio, and eventually things like robotics and action, the models stop being just very sophisticated language processors and start becoming systems that can ground their understanding in something closer to the full richness of reality. A huge amount of what we know, as people, isn't written down anywhere. It's in how things look, how they move, how they sound, how objects behave when you interact with them. Text only gives you a compressed, secondhand version of that.

So I expect that as these systems become genuinely multimodal, not just bolting a vision module onto a language model, but really integrated, people are going to have a very different experience of them. You'll be able to show it what you're doing, talk to it naturally, have it watch a video and understand what's going on in a deep way. And I think that will feel qualitatively different. It'll shift how people perceive these systems, from a clever chatbot to something that actually understands the world in a way that's more like the way we do.

And historically, the landmarks people remember aren't always the biggest technical steps. They're the moments where the public's intuition about what these systems are suddenly changes. I think full multimodality is likely to be one of those moments.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodal inputs let systems ground their understanding in the richness of reality, while text provides only a narrow, compressed account of human experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look at what's happened so far, the systems have been largely trained on text, and that's been enormously successful, because there's a huge amount of knowledge encoded in text. But it's a very narrow slice of the world. When you think about how a human understands things, we're grounded in vision, in sound, in the physical world around us. There's a lot of structure that's just not in the text, or is only implicitly there.

So when these systems start taking in images and video and audio in a serious way, not as an add-on but as part of the core model, I think people are going to be surprised at how much more they seem to understand. The models will be able to look at a scene and reason about it, watch something happening and explain it, and that's going to change how people perceive them. Right now you interact with a language model and it feels like a very clever thing that's read a lot. When it can actually see what you're seeing, and talk about it, that's going to feel qualitatively different. I think that's the kind of moment people remember, the way they remember when the chatbots suddenly started working.

And there's a deeper reason too. If you want something that approaches general intelligence, it has to be able to handle the kinds of inputs that humans handle. A lot of what we'd want these systems to do, in the physical world, in robotics, in just helping someone with their everyday life, requires that grounding. So I see multimodality as not just a feature but as a step towards a more complete form of understanding. The capabilities will unlock a lot of applications, but I think the real thing is that the models will start to have a much richer internal picture of how the world works.

r001.rationale: The response says text captures only a narrow slice of the world and that vision, sound, and physical-world grounding will give multimodal models a richer understanding.

astra-6.text:
Because language is only one part of how we understand the world. It’s an extraordinarily useful part, and you can learn a tremendous amount from text. But there are things that are very difficult to convey in words that become obvious when you see them happening.

If you watch somebody manipulate an unfamiliar object, you can learn something about its shape, how its parts move, and what it might be useful for. A description of that interaction will inevitably leave a lot out. A system that can learn directly from video and sound, and connect that with language, has access to a much richer source of information.

The interesting step is when those capabilities work together. You could show a system something you’re trying to fix, talk through the problem, and have it follow what you’re doing as the situation changes. That’s a different kind of interaction from typing a question and getting an answer.

Now, that doesn’t automatically solve reasoning or planning. But I think it will make the progress very tangible. People will feel that the system understands more of the world they’re actually in, rather than just the words they use to describe it.

r001.rationale: The response says video and sound provide a richer source of information than text alone, helping systems understand more of the world people inhabit.

sol-6.1.text:
Because language is only one part of the world, right? A huge amount of what we understand comes from seeing things, hearing things, interacting with them, and learning how all those things fit together. If you want a more general intelligence, you want it to be able to bring those sources of information together.

Imagine an AI that can watch what you’re doing, understand what you’re saying, and have a conversation with you about it. You could show it something you’re trying to fix, or ask it to explain something happening in front of you. That’s a much more natural way to interact than having to translate everything into a text prompt.

So I think it will be memorable partly because of the capabilities, but also because of how it feels to use. When a system can understand the situation you’re in and respond appropriately, it starts to feel like a much more general assistant.

r001.rationale: The response says language is only one part of the world and that combining visual, auditory, and interactive information supports broader understanding than text prompts alone.
